justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 1278 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to around 1300 at one month. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily to the most recent observed price level, with only a slight drift component built in based on recent short-term momentum. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for a small positive bias reflecting the general tendency of this asset class to appreciate modestly over time, while also accounting for mean-reversion pressures that limit how far prices can stray quickly. At the one-month horizon, the point estimate continues that gentle upward slope, but the case for any specific direction weakens considerably as the forecast horizon extends and more macroeconomic variables come into play.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because intraday and overnight price moves tend to be bounded under normal market conditions, and there is limited time for new fundamental information to materially reprice the asset. By one week, the interval nearly doubles in width, capturing the possibility of scheduled economic data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment. At one month, the interval widens further still, reflecting the full range of macroeconomic scenarios that could plausibly unfold, including shifts in inflation expectations, liquidity conditions, and global risk appetite.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in global risk sentiment — triggered by an unexpected geopolitical shock, a major credit event, or a sharp hawkish pivot from a central bank — could push prices well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Liquidity crises or forced selling in correlated asset classes can amplify moves far beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest. On the upside, a surprise easing of monetary policy, a significant de-escalation of geopolitical tensions, or a stronger-than-expected demand signal could drive prices above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for such a narrative to build and attract capital flows.
